To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
fPSA, the most abundant form of PSA, can be measured with a high degree of specificity by using a monoclonal antibody (mAb) that recognizes a unique epitope on fPSA.

(1) the ratio of fPSA to total PSA (fPSAT) is a better predictor of prostate cancer than total PSA alone, and that (2) the combination of fPSA with other prostate-specific markers, especially hK2, will improve prostate cancer detection and will help to avoid the unnecessary prostate biopsied in men with benign prostate disease.
fPSA, PSA-ACT, and hK2 can be used to improve the detection of prostate cancer, and that hK2 can also be used to improve prostate cancer staging.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a new approach to the study of the molecular forms of the prostate cancer.
the development and clinical validation of new biomarkers for the early detection and management of prostate cancer.
the development of a novel approach to the study of the molecular form of PSA.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the use of the PSA isoforms, fPSA and PSA-ACT, has not yet been proven to be clinically superior to the use of the total PSA level for prostate cancer detection in the general population.
PSA is the best available marker for prostate cancer detection, but it is far from perfect and needs improvement.

fPSA and PSA-ACT are clinically useful for the early detection and management of prostate cancer, but that the role of other PSA forms, such PSA bound to alpha-1-antitrypsin (ACT) and the pro-form of PSA (proPSA) remains to be determined.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the use of PSA as a biomarker for prostate cancer detection has been challenged by the discovery of its molecular forms and other kallikerins.
fPSA is an excellent marker for distinguishing benign prostate disease from prostate cancer.
the clinical utility of PSA has been significantly enhanced by the measurement of fPSA.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the use of molecular forms of PSA in conjunction with hK2 can improve prostate cancer detection and reduce the number of unnecessary biopsies.
the use of PSA as a screening test for prostate cancer has been disappointing because of its low specificity.

fPSA and other PSA forms can improve the specificity of PSA testing and thus reduce unnecessary biopsies, and that additional kallikrekins can improve the sensitivity of PSA testing and reduce the number of missed cancers.
